Leaders: transformation should not be your focus

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1364 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that in his 1980 book Managing in Turbulent Times, management guru Peter Drucker wrote, “The greatest danger in times of turbulence is not the turbulence; it is to act with yesterday’s logic.” This seems obvious.
  • Recent findings suggest that in his 1980 book Managing in Turbulent Times, management guru Peter Drucker wrote, “The greatest danger in times of turbulence is not the turbulence; it is to act with yesterday’s logic.” This seems obvious.
  • In a recent development, it may be tempting to think that the other side of turbulence is overhauling the organization in a major transformation effort.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in his 1980 book Managing in Turbulent Times, management guru Peter Drucker wrote, “The greatest danger in times of turbulence is not the turbulence; it is to act with yesterday’s logic.” This seems obvious. But more often than not, businesses lean into safe, tried and true, old-school thinking as their life raft during uncertain times. Consider Nvidia, initially defending keeping Jensen Huang in place as CEO amidst accusations of major ethical missteps. It may be tempting to think that the other side of turbulence is overhauling the organization in a major transformation effort. But Geoff Tuff and Steve Goldbach, who are leaders in Deloitte’s sustainability practice, have a different take on moving through organizational turbulence. They believe that large-scale transformation is not the right focus. In fact, their research and experience show that organizations who focus on transformation tend to fail. What they offer instead is an alternative view that is compellingly explored in their book Hone: How Purposeful Leaders Defy Drift. Cumulatively, Geoff and Steve have decades of experience working with Fortune 500 companies that end up drifting in the process of trying to transform. When I recently spoke with them they shared that “drift” is the unintentional, imperceptible shift that leaves an organization uncompetitive because leaders fail to make micro-adjustments along the way. The solution? Hone: make small, intentional continuous adjustments to stay on course rather than wait until a massive disruption is necessary. Here are my three biggest takeaways from our conversation. 1. Honing is the antidote to failed transformation. Broad-scale transformations carry a 70% failure rate because humans naturally resist drastic change. This leads to organizational “tissue rejection.” Instead replace massive transformation with continuous “honing” to prevent drift. Geoff’s pastime and love of sailing have clearly influenced their perspective. Because just like adjusting a boat’s autopilot to account for winds and currents, leaders should focus on honing (for example, micro-adjustments in leadership style, accountability, KPI’s, etc.)  to stay on course rather than wait until a massive, disruptive transformation is required. 2. AI can help identify where honing is needed. Invisible drift can be made visible because AI can detect subtle patterns and organizational drift that are otherwise invisible to the human eye, enabling managers to address challenges proactively. An AI enabled organizational network analysis can track thousands of interactions over time (such as email and Slack messages about meetings). For example, it can spot if an engineering team’s contact with the product team has decreased over 30% over multiple quarters. A 2021 study published in Nature Human Behaviour demonstrated that a 60,000 person Microsoft team’s collaboration efforts decreased when the team went remote. Employees engaged in more intra-team communication than inter-team communication. AI can serve as an early warning system, surface weak signals and alert leaders about a future they may not want so that they can course correct. 3. Honing demands deep behavioral curiosity. The good news is that we can adopt a “honing mindset.” A successful “honer” walks through the world constructively dissatisfied with current processes. And not because they’re unhappy, but because they’re more critically curious and attuned to identify design flaws, eliminate waste, and continuously tweak systems. Organizations change when the individuals within them start behaving differently. To drive that change, leaders must practice self-awareness and empathy to understand what truly motivates their teams. If you’re wondering how to make honing a regular behavioral practice on your own team, start by inviting someone in from the outside. It should be a person from a different team or even a different industry who can cast a bird’s eye view on your operations and ask the “naive questions.” In design thinking we call this “lateral thinking.” Then, collect three of their questions and keep them as regular trackers that you continuously go back to asking yourself and your team as navigational tools. Because just as it’s easier to spot a ship that’s going off course from the shoreline, an outsider can help spark the necessary micro-adjustments to ensure that you’re honing- not drifting.

  • According to this latest report, prosecutors urged a federal judge to deny Alfozan’s request to be released on bail while the investigation is ongoing, fearing that Alfozan might flee before trial “given his relatively weak ties to the US and the considerable […] connections he has in his native Saudi Arabia.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that last month, a former OpenAI employee with ties to Saudi Arabia was arrested for bugging conference rooms in the company. Today, Bloomberg reports that prosecutors in the case uncovered hundreds of recordings, dozens of which were meetings and conversations dating as far back as September. Prosecutors believe some recordings may contain sensitive information that can be regarded as trade secrets, the dispersion of which could be a threat to US national security.

Recent findings suggest that in October, we covered how Abdulrahman Alfozan, a former OpenAI employee, was arrested for installing a covert listening device behind the manufacturer's executive conference room television using a Seeed Xiao ESP32-S3. The device was discovered days later, with investigations linking it to Alfozan and subsequently leading to his arrest and removal from the company.

According to this latest report, prosecutors urged a federal judge to deny Alfozan’s request to be released on bail while the investigation is ongoing, fearing that Alfozan might flee before trial “given his relatively weak ties to the US and the considerable […] connections he has in his native Saudi Arabia.”.

Industry observers note that prosecutors have stated, “Thus far, the government has located hundreds of audio files on the defendant’s personal computer, including dozens of recordings of meetings or conversations that occurred at OpenAI throughout September 2026, many of which involve discussions of what may be trade secrets,” as reported by Bloomberg. The court filing also notes that Alfozan kept audio files and AI-generated transcripts on his computer, with some recordings uploaded to Dropbox, “meticulously categorized by date and renamed according to the content of the recording.” Prosecutors also found a collections of images of a "strategic partnership" document marked as confidential on Alfozan's confiscated phone.

The filing also states, “At the same time as he was secretly recording, cataloging, and transcribing dozens of meetings concerning (among other things) OpenAI’s partnerships and capabilities, the defendant was in frequent communication with various people affiliated with the Saudi government.” However, Alfozan denies stealing trade secrets from OpenAI for Saudi Arabia, with his lawyer arguing that Alfozan “has no special or covert ties to the Saudi government,” in a separate court filing on Friday.

Sources indicate that according to the October 27 indictment, he is charged with interception of oral communications, not theft of trade secrets or economic espionage, as with sharing trade secrets with another government. Alfozan requested to set his bond at $1 million, but this could be denied at the hearing set for Tuesday; additional charges could also follow if the investigation finds out what Alfozan is doing, or plans to do, with the recordings and to whom he would send them.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that AI is changing nearly every aspect of the workplace—but especially entry-level jobs, to the point where Gen Z is calling for millennials (who are only in their 30s and 40s) to retire to make room.
  • According to recent reports, AI is changing nearly every aspect of the workplace—but especially entry-level jobs, to the point where Gen Z is calling for millennials (who are only in their 30s and 40s) to retire to make room.
  • A recent survey of nearly 7,000 workers, managers, and executives found that 51% believe AI is reducing early-career opportunities, while 49% say tasks that traditionally helped employees build work experience are increasingly being handled by AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that AI is changing nearly every aspect of the workplace—but especially entry-level jobs, to the point where Gen Z is calling for millennials (who are only in their 30s and 40s) to retire to make room. Many are placing the blame on AI for making tasks in many entry-level jobs outdated; data seems to back that up. A recent survey of nearly 7,000 workers, managers, and executives found that 51% believe AI is reducing early-career opportunities, while 49% say tasks that traditionally helped employees build work experience are increasingly being handled by AI. Another shows that entry-level listings have plummeted 35% since 2023; another suggests entry-level jobs in Upcoming York City have been cut in half. That means the pressure is on for early-career candidates to show employers what they can bring to a role beyond their ability to use AI tools. A catch-22 emerges: many employers increasingly turn to AI, yet many also want candidates who can think independently, come up with original ideas, recognize when to put the technology aside and trust their own judgment. Indeed, many young workers find themselves in a tricky-to-navigate, even unfair entry-level job market. Luckily, there are tips that can make you stand out in a labor market that both increasingly relies on AI, and that also demands workers show employers the human skills they’re looking for. Don’t let AI write your resume for you Sure, AI can be a helpful writing tool: it can help you brainstorm, organize your experience, even give you a first draft. But if every candidate is using AI to write their application, it can become harder to show what makes you different. According to Amitoj Sandhu, Manager of Global Early Talent at HR platform Dayforce, employers are starting to see more applications that all sound alike. “Every single profile looks the same. They all are the same on the paper, so it becomes really hard for us to shortlist them and present in front of leaders,” he states. Sandhu says AI is a useful starting point, but candidates need to be able to use their own voice, and  stand behind what they submit. After all, if AI is writing your resume for you, when it comes time for the interview, “will you be able to validate the results?” he says. Sandhu recommends preparing two or three strong examples from internships, school projects, or extracurricular activities that you can actually speak to authentically without farming everything out to ChatGPT. Then, be ready to walk an interviewer through those experiences and what you learned from them. With fewer entry-level roles apparently available, layering this in can make your application pop. Do use AI in your cover letter, but with caution “AI can be a great tool for writing a better cover letter. It can help candidates organize their ideas, communicate more clearly and make meaningful connections between their own interests and the company they’re applying to,” says Dan Kejsefman, Talent Director at Avature, a software development company. He says AI can raise the bar in terms of an application’s quality—but at the same time, “the motivation behind it still needs to be genuine.”  “I’d encourage candidates to start with their own reasons for wanting the job: What interests them about the company? What would they like to learn? What experiences or interests connect them to the opportunity? Then use AI to help communicate those ideas more effectively,” he says. The crucial thing is being able to explain and stand behind what’s in your cover letter. “AI can help you tell your story better,” he says, “but the story still has to be yours.” Use AI tools where you can—many jobs will expect you to use them to some extent, anyway—but standing out in an increasingly crowded entry-level field means tapping into what makes you, you. Don’t leave your curiosity at home According to Sandhu, when it comes time for the interview, curiosity is one of the biggest qualities employers look for. Missing that in an interview is “kind of a red flag for us,” Sandhu says. Sure, one way to demonstrate this is by researching the employer before the interview, and developing a genuine understanding of what the company does and the industry it operates in. But preparation is only part of it. Kejsefman says candidates also need to show genuine interest in the conversation, rather than simply relying on a list of questions prepared with AI during your interview practice. “AI can help candidates research a company, understand a role, and prepare thoughtful questions. That’s useful, and I wouldn’t discourage it,” Kejsefman explains. “But there’s a difference between asking an impressive question, and actually being interested in understanding the answer.” For example, curious candidates listen carefully, ask follow-up questions and try to understand why things work the way they do. That’s a timeless strategy, regardless of AI or not. Young workers “don’t necessarily have all the answers, and that’s perfectly fine, especially early in their careers. What matters is whether they show a real desire to learn and understand,” Kejsefman says. Do bring your own judgment to the work Sandhu says employers want candidates who can question the information AI provides, apply their own judgment and build on what the technology produces. Think of a software developer who might use ChatGPT to generate code, but still needs to determine whether it makes sense or meets the requirements or passes the right tests. Human judgment, after all, has long been touted as something that will still prove crucial in the AI era—in fact, as more decisions get outsourced to robots, it becomes even more valuable. “Can you use your own judgment to evaluate a response you get from AI? Can you build on that context? That’s what we’re looking for,” Sandhu says. In fields such as communications and journalism, employers still want to see creativity and original ideas rather than generic content generated by AI. “They want to look at how you think and what kind of ideas you can spark, not just all the generic ideas AI is producing,” Sandhu says. Kejsefman says AI adoption is still uneven across organizations, creating an opportunity for early-career professionals. As AI takes on more workplace tasks, your ability to bring your own ideas, judgment and perspective to the work can help you stand out—especially when looking to break into a field or organization. And that experience doesn’t have to come from a traditional job. Kejsefman encourages recent graduates to draw on those other past experiences, like university projects or volunteering—even personal projects or side gigs, which a lot of Gen Z already has anyway. “They need examples of situations where they’ve taken initiative, faced a problem, learned something new, or adapted when things didn’t go as expected,” Kejsefman says. “For someone starting their career, demonstrating that mindset can be much more valuable than presenting a perfectly polished result.” Make no mistake—for new workers in the workplace, it’s rough out there. 📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s bad enough you have to sleep on the pull-out couch for a few days, but then come the questions.
  • It’s bad enough you have to sleep on the pull-out couch for a few days, but then come the questions.
  • If the topic of homeownership—and, more pointedly, why you don’t yet own a home—comes up at Thanksgiving, here’s a stat to keep your pestering relatives at bay.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s bad enough you have to sleep on the pull-out couch for a few days, but then come the questions. If the topic of homeownership—and, more pointedly, why you don’t yet own a home—comes up at Thanksgiving, here’s a stat to keep your pestering relatives at bay. A household today earning a median income would need to save for 10.5 years to have enough for a 10% down payment on a median-priced home—that’s more than three times longer than in the 1980s, according to a newly introduced report from Realtor.com. While your relatives may bemoan the double-digit mortgage rates of the 1980s, homes on the market were relatively more affordable. That’s because the surge in home prices, and especially in recent years, has far outpaced the rise in wages, which is keeping many prospective homebuyers on the sidelines, according to the Austin-based real estate site. “The reality is that today’s aspiring buyers face a different housing market than generations before,” Hannah Jones, senior economist at Realtor.com, remarked in a statement. And it’s not just that home prices have outpaced wage growth, homebuyers are also facing rising costs for insurance and homeowners association (HOA) fees that are stretching their budgets, she added. “The path to homeownership has become increasingly difficult.” In the 1980s, the median-priced home was selling for roughly 3.2 times the typical annual household income at the time, according to Realtor.com. Today, shoppers are trying to squeeze into a market where homes are selling for 4.8 times the typical household income. It’s no wonder, then, that so many younger people are living at home for longer to save up for a down payment when a first-time homebuyer is now 40 years old. The broader markets are seeing red today, primarily led lower by yet another steep selloff in technology and artificial intelligence stocks. But one company nearly as far from those sectors as you can get is seeing its share price surge by over 10% today: the discount retailer Dollar Tree. Here’s what you need to know. What’s happened? This morning, the discount retail chain Dollar Tree, Inc. (Nasdaq: DLTR) reported its third-quarter fiscal 2026 results, which cover the three-month period ending October 31. The most salient metrics from those results are as follows: Net sales: $5.1 billion Adjusted earnings per share (EPS): $1.16 Comparable store net sales: up 4.6% Foot traffic increase: 3.8% New stores: 84 Total stores: 9,511 To put those financials in perspective, LSEG analysts estimated $5.04 billion in net sales and earnings per share of 91 cents, notes Reuters. Announcing the company’s Q3 results, Dollar Tree CEO Mike Creedon said, “Our third quarter results show the strength of Dollar Tree’s value proposition and the progress we’ve made to improve the customer experience. Comp traffic accelerated to 3.8% and drove comparable sales above the high end of our outlook. Our broader assortment, better stores and stronger customer engagement give shoppers more reasons to choose Dollar Tree and come back more often.” Why are Dollar Tree’s shares surging? After announcing its Q3, DLTR stock surged—one of the few to do so today on Wall Street. Dollar Tree’s price jump comes down to a few factors, both of which seem to have pleased investors, based on the company’s share price. The first was the net sales and earnings per share beat. Net sales increased by 6.9% versus the same quarter a year earlier. This was helped by a 4.6% increase in comparable net store sales. Those comps were driven by a 3.8% increase in foot traffic and a 0.8% increase in the amount people spend on an average ticket. In other words, most of the comp increase was not driven by higher tickets, but by increased foot traffic—which is exactly what you want as you enter the final quarter of the year: the all-key holiday period. In addition to favorable quarterly results, another factor that buoyed investors’ view of the company was its full-year fiscal 2026 outlook. Dollar Tree increased its full-year earnings per share range to between $8.05 and $8.25. That was up from its prior range of $7.70 to $8.05. DLTR’s up more than 60% in six months As of the time of this writing, DLTR shares are presently trading up 11% to $154.41 on the back of its Q3 results. That’s an exceptional one-day jump for a discount retailer, but it goes to show the faith investors currently have in the company, which may be one of the few to benefit from an inflation-wary consumer. As prices rise, people tend to cut back on discretionary spending, which can cause downward pressure on retailer shares. But as everyday costs get higher, consumers also tend to shop around for the best price for essentials and everyday items. Dollar Tree has a low-cost pricing structure (many items cost around $1.25, with higher-priced items selling for between $3 and $7) that appeals to cash-strapped consumers operating in an economy where sticker prices at higher-end retailers seem increasingly out of reach. While the company’s roughly 11% share price jump today (as of the time of this writing) is impressive, looking back a little further reveals even better stock price growth. In the past month alone, DLTR shares are up 22%, and over the past six months, DLTR shares are up 61%.

Recent findings suggest that A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) app is usually drawn as a language model plus a vector database. When it goes live, the part that fails first is rarely the retrieval. It is GPU memory on the generation model, because a model that loads fine for one request can run out of memory when several users send long questions at once.

This article indicates how to estimate that limit before you deploy, with a short script you can run, and then covers what else in the pipeline can slow responses down.

Serving a model takes more than its weights. The GPU also holds:.

the key-value (KV) cache, which grows with the length of every active request.

activations and batching overhead.

memory used by the inference runtime itself.

SitePoint's guide to running a local LLM on 10GB of VRAM makes the same point for a single desktop GPU: the usable budget is the total VRAM minus overhead, and the KV cache grows with the context window, so the real model budget is smaller than the number on the box.

Recent findings suggest that for a RAG service, the KV cache matters even more. Retrieved passages are pasted into the prompt, so every request carries a long context, and every concurrent request holds its own cache.

Industry observers note that the cache size per token depends on the model's architecture: two tensors (keys and values) for every layer, for every KV head. This script turns those numbers into a rough limit on concurrent requests:.

def kv_bytes_per_token(layers, kv_heads, head_dim, dtype_bytes=2):.

# Keys and values, for every layer, for one token.

return 2 *layers *kv_heads *head_dim *dtype_bytes.

def max_concurrent(vram_gb, weights_gb, ctx_tokens, per_token, reserve_gb=2.0):.

budget = (vram_gb - weights_gb - reserve_gb) * GIB.

return int(budget // (ctx_tokens * per_token)).

per_token = kv_bytes_per_token(32, 8, 128).

print(per_token // 1024, "KiB per token").

for ctx in (4096, 8192, 16384):.

n = max_concurrent(24, 16, ctx, per_token).

print(ctx, "tokens ->", n, "concurrent requests").

For a 24 GB GPU holding about 16 GB of fp16 weights with 2 GB kept in reserve, it prints:.

4096 tokens -> 12 concurrent requests.

8192 tokens -> 6 concurrent requests.

16384 tokens -> 3 concurrent requests.

Sources indicate that the numbers are estimates. Real runtimes add their own overhead, and the architecture values come from the model's configuration file, so read them from the model you actually use. The pattern is what matters: doubling the context length halves the number of requests that fit. A RAG prompt that stuffs in ten retrieved chunks costs real capacity.

Industry observers note that serving runtimes do not simply crash when the cache is full. The vLLM documentation on optimization and tuning explains that when KV cache space is insufficient for all batched requests, the engine preempts some of them and recomputes them later, which can hurt end-to-end latency. Its suggested remedies include giving the cache more memory, reducing the number of concurrent sequences or batched tokens, or sharding the model across GPUs.

So the symptom of undersizing is often not an error. It is slow, uneven responses under load. Test with realistic prompt lengths and several simultaneous users, not a single request.

It has been revealed that embedding and ingestion have a different profile from generation. Embedding is often lighter than serving a large language model, and some teams run it on CPU. Document parsing, chunking and tokenization also run on CPU, so a fast GPU cannot make up for a slow CPU upstream. SitePoint's tutorial on a local RAG system for private documents walks through chunking, embeddings, vector storage and reranking, and is a good map of which stages run where.

RAM: vector indexes, document loaders and caches all live in system memory, so large collections need more of it.

Recent findings suggest that storage: model files, indexes, logs and backups add up. Fast storage shortens model loading and re-indexing.

Network: if the vector database, application server and model server sit in different places, latency adds to every request.

According to recent reports, two layouts are common. A single instance runs everything and is simplest for prototypes and internal tools. Separated services put ingestion and retrieval on smaller machines and keep the GPU for generation, which scales better as traffic grows.

It has been revealed that memory estimates only hold if the GPU memory is really yours. On a shared or time-sliced GPU, other workloads can take memory and compute away from your service, which makes capacity hard to proposal. Hosting providers describe this in different terms, such as passthrough, vGPU, MIG and time-slicing. For a view of how one GPU hosting provider explains those allocation methods, GPU Mart's GPU virtualization guide compares them. It is a hosting tech giant's page, so confirm any provider's claims about isolation and performance with your own load test.

Whatever provider you choose, ask these questions:.

Is the physical GPU assigned to you exclusively, or partitioned or time-sliced?

Do you have root access to install your own drivers, CUDA libraries and containers?

Which minimum commitments, regions and support terms apply?

Sources indicate that A small stack can run as a handful of containers: an API service for request handling and prompt assembly, an ingestion worker, a vector database and a model server. Keeping them separate lets you monitor each one's memory and CPU use and move the heavy one to bigger hardware without rewriting the rest.

Recent findings suggest that for a service that stays up all month, a fixed monthly term is easier to forecast than hourly capacity. Hourly capacity suits testing quantization settings or processing a one-off document batch.

Is GPU memory always the bottleneck for RAG?

Not always. Generation usually hits memory first, but slow parsing, a small CPU or a distant vector database can dominate response time.

Does quantization solve the memory problem?

Recent findings suggest that it shrinks the weights, but the KV cache still grows with context length and concurrency. Test with your real prompt sizes.

Should embeddings run on the GPU?

It depends on volume. Small workloads can run on CPU, while a large ingestion job may benefit from a GPU for a limited time.

Size a RAG service for the worst realistic moment, not the single-request demo. Estimate the KV cache from the model's architecture, remember that long retrieved contexts reduce how many requests fit, watch for preemption under load, keep CPU, RAM, storage and network in the strategy, and find out whether the GPU is exclusive or shared. The script above is small, but it turns a vague worry about memory into numbers you can check.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While there is still no recipe for becoming a globally recognized musician, there is one thing that is consistently getting artists on the charts: TikTok. TikTok’s recent 2026 Music Impact Report found that 94% of songs that entered the Billboard top 200 chart this year went viral on TikTok first. The link is stronger than before: in 2024, TikTok found that 84% of songs on the charts had gone viral on the platform first,  up ten percentage points in two years. TikTok virality also affects how long a song stays on the chart. The report also found that tracks that went viral on the platform stayed on the charts for four times longer than those that didn’t catch a moment of popularity on the platform. For instance, songs that had a viral moment on TikTok would spend eight weeks on Billboard charts, as opposed to just two weeks for non-viral hits. But the charts are not the only metric artists use to measure their success and growth, their performance on streaming platforms matters too. The report also found that TikTok virality influences streaming, with 74% of the fastest-growing artists on streaming platforms saw their streams rise alongside their views on TikTok. Sienna Spiro is among the breakthrough artists who rose to fame through the platform, starting her career singing songs to a small audience on TikTok, eventually landing on the VMA stage this year singing her hit song Great Expectations. While a relatively small artist just a year ago, she found a viral moment in her song Die on This Hill, with millions of fans using the sound for their TikToks, giving her recognition beyond the platform. Additionally, the platform’s latest “add to music app” feature, which lets users connect their TikTok to their streaming service to automatically save songs from videos to their playlists, contributed to Spiro’s streaming success. According to the report, millions of users used the feature to save the single to their music apps. Spiro’s viral hit led her to enter the top 20 of the Billboard Hot 100, where it stayed for 13 weeks.

We recently reviewed the GO27Q24G and came away impressed with its value, video processing, and brightness. Why your HSA needs a succession plan

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1791 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Health savings accounts are usually discussed in the context of their trifecta of tax benefits: pretax money going in, tax-free compounding while the funds are inside the account, and tax-free withdrawals for qualified healthcare expenditures.But HSAs have their limits.
  • It has been revealed that health savings accounts are usually discussed in the context of their trifecta of tax benefits: pretax money going in, tax-free compounding while the funds are inside the account, and tax-free withdrawals for qualified healthcare expenditures.But HSAs have their limits.
  • According to recent reports, whereas tax-sheltered retirement account owners will pay taxes on the dollars they put into a retirement account (Roth) or on their withdrawals (traditional tax-deferred), HSAs are a unicorn account type—the funds are tax-free every step of the way, provided you spend the money on qualified healthcare expenses.Those tax benefits are magnified for people who pay their healthcare expenses out of pocket, invest in long-term investment assets, and are in higher tax brackets.Given those prodigious tax benefits, an HSA investor would have a bigger balance than a person investing in an IRA, 401(k), or taxable brokerage account, assuming the same contribution amounts, rates of return, tax rates, and holding periods.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Health savings accounts are usually discussed in the context of their trifecta of tax benefits: pretax money going in, tax-free compounding while the funds are inside the account, and tax-free withdrawals for qualified healthcare expenditures.But HSAs have their limits. The HSA’s tax benefits effectively cease upon the account owner’s death, or the death of his or her spouse if that person is the beneficiary.That makes it crucial to have a succession initiative for your HSA: a plan to encourage tax-free spending during your lifetime (and your spouse’s, if you have one), as well as naming the correct beneficiary for the account to maximize the tax benefits. HSAs give during your lifetime . . . Whereas tax-sheltered retirement account owners will pay taxes on the dollars they put into a retirement account (Roth) or on their withdrawals (traditional tax-deferred), HSAs are a unicorn account type—the funds are tax-free every step of the way, provided you spend the money on qualified healthcare expenses.Those tax benefits are magnified for people who pay their healthcare expenses out of pocket, invest in long-term investment assets, and are in higher tax brackets.Given those prodigious tax benefits, an HSA investor would have a bigger balance than a person investing in an IRA, 401(k), or taxable brokerage account, assuming the same contribution amounts, rates of return, tax rates, and holding periods. That’s because investors in those other account types pay taxes along the way: at time of contribution (Roth), during accumulation (taxable), and/or at time of withdrawal (taxable, traditional tax-deferred). . . . And take after death If your spouse is the designated beneficiary of your HSA, the HSA becomes theirs after your death, and the tax benefits continue. They can continue to take tax-free withdrawals for qualified healthcare expenses.But if a person other than your spouse inherits the HSA, the account becomes less attractive than the other key account types mentioned before. An HSA inherited by a nonspouse beneficiary effectively ceases to be an HSA upon the account owner’s death, and all of its tax benefits go away at that time. Moreover, the nonspouse beneficiary will need to include the inherited HSA amount in their income and pay taxes on it.The tax treatment of an HSA inherited by a nonspouse beneficiary is a bit worse than the tax treatment of other major account types that nonspouse beneficiaries might inherit. Heirs enjoy tax-free withdrawals on inherited Roth accounts. Traditional IRA beneficiaries owe taxes, but they at least enjoy some flexibility on the timing of their withdrawals and tax bills. Heirs inheriting taxable accounts have it even better, in that their cost basis becomes whatever the account holdings’ values were on the date of your death. You need a plan for handling your HSA That meh tax treatment on HSAs inherited by nonspouse beneficiaries highlights the value of having a plan to maximize your HSA’s long-term tax benefits. Step 1: Get a system for spending from it Spending from the HSA during your and your spouse’s lifetimes is key, so every HSA owner needs a spending plan. That’s true whether you’re paying healthcare expenses as you incur them or investing the funds for retirement.If you’ve been paying your healthcare costs out of pocket in an effort to allow your account to grow, you can later use the HSA for non-healthcare expenses, provided you have receipts to substantiate those previous out-of-pocket healthcare costs. Ideally, you’d scan and document those expenditures as you incur them. If you’re a married person who’s overseeing your household’s HSA, make sure your spouse understands the withdrawal rules, where to find receipts, and how to submit them to the HSA provider. Step 2: Assign the correct beneficiaries Next, give care to naming beneficiaries. If you’re married, your spouse is a sensible beneficiary for the HSA; as noted earlier, they will be able to take over ownership of the account after your death and keep its full tax benefits during their lifetime.Nonspouse beneficiaries won’t receive the same favorable tax treatment. However, if you think a nonspouse beneficiary still will benefit from the money, that’s probably a good enough reason to leave them the HSA. But other accounts should take precedence.A charity can also make an excellent HSA beneficiary, as the charity won’t need to pay taxes on that amount. That strategy can be particularly appropriate for single people who are charitably inclined, or for surviving spouses. If you’re married, consider making your spouse the primary beneficiary and a charity the secondary. Step 3: Make sure your beneficiaries understand the rules about HSAs If your spouse will inherit your HSA, be sure to underscore the value of liquidating the account during his or her lifetime.While it’s generally not advisable for a nonspouse beneficiary to inherit an HSA, if that’s your plan, it’s key to let your loved ones know that they can reduce the taxable amount in the HSA by paying any of your unpaid medical bills from the HSA. They just need to pay those bills out of your HSA within a year of your death. This article was provided to The Associated Press by Morningstar. Tech Report: GrapheneOS reveals off how it plans RCS support without Google Messages

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (293 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: 9to5google

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • RCS is coming to GrapheneOS without Google Messages, as a proof-of-concept app shows how the privacy-focused version Android can implement the messaging standard.
  • As virtually all Android phones and now iPhone support RCS messaging, the standard is key to communication in 2026.
  • It’s a problem that Graphene’s developers have been trying to work out for a while now, and it seems progress is being made.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

RCS is coming to GrapheneOS without Google Messages, as a proof-of-concept app shows how the privacy-focused version Android can implement the messaging standard.

As virtually all Android phones and now iPhone support RCS messaging, the standard is key to communication in 2026. But GrapheneOS users, by default, are still stuck with SMS/MMS as RCS is typically locked behind Google Messages on Android.

It’s a problem that Graphene’s developers have been trying to work out for a while now, and it seems progress is being made. A proof-of-concept messaging app with RCS was shared on Twitter/X, showing Graphene’s RCS implementation working with both Google Messages and iOS with end-to-end encryption and full features including typing indicators and reactions.

While this app skips the need to use Google Messages directly, the app does still use Google’s services as most carriers rely on Google for RCS. GrapheneOS still needs a sandboxed version of Google Play, for now, for this to work, but the developers say that a standalone version for carriers that support Google-less RCS will be coming.

We made a proof of concept RCS messaging app. It already has end-to-end encryption with MLS compatible with Google Messages and iOS, typing indicators, delivery/read receipts, reactions and media/file sharing. We'll use what was learned to integrate RCS into our Messaging app. pic.twitter.com/jzCTCCKrIQ.

There’s still no firm timeline for this newly introduced RCS support on GrapheneOS, but Google Messages can still be used in the meantime.

#92754. Why your boss can basically fire you for anything—and why it’s not like that outside the U.S.

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2352 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

Why your boss can basically fire you for anything—and why it’s not like that outside the U.S.

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2352 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We’ve all seen the scene play out in media: A character stands up at work, dramatically declares they quit, and walks out of the office for the last time.
  • We’ve all seen the scene play out in media: A character stands up at work, dramatically declares they quit, and walks out of the office for the last time.
  • Mostly because it goes both ways: an employer can axe you at the drop of a hat, in theory—even without a warning, PIP, or other chance to improve.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We’ve all seen the scene play out in media: A character stands up at work, dramatically declares they quit, and walks out of the office for the last time. While many people will surely empathize with that desire, the reason why a sudden resignation is possible in the U.S. isn’t as great as such a display makes it out to be. Mostly because it goes both ways: an employer can axe you at the drop of a hat, in theory—even without a warning, PIP, or other chance to improve. The U.S. has something called at-will employment, which means that you can leave—or lose—your job without giving any notice. A job that’s at-will “can end at any moment, for good reason, bad reason, or no reason at all, and with no procedural mandates,” notes Gali Racabi, an assistant professor at Cornell’s School of Industrial and Labor Relations and an associated faculty member of Cornell Law School. Right now, at-will employment is the law of the land in Washington, D.C., and every U.S. state except Montana. “This makes work in the US really easy to sever,” Racabi says. He adds: “The at-will rule is a travesty, and a mark of moral flaw in our economic order. We need to do away with it ASAP.”  Critiques of at-will employment Despite being the default in America—a country whose culture is associated with entrepreneurialism, independence and one that favors employers without much safety-net protection for workers—at-will employment causes a number of concerns. Most prominent, perhaps, is a person suddenly losing their income and the many repercussions that can come with that. The practice is also especially risky in the U.S., where individuals often rely on their job for necessary benefits like healthcare—something many other nations provide outside of employment, Racabi says. Say, for instance, a person has an operation scheduled for next week and gets laid off today. Suddenly, they don’t have coverage for a necessary procedure. That’s a more extreme example. But even losing health insurance without a major medical issue coming up, and no time to find an alternative, can have devastating repercussions around the cost of medicine, seeing a doctor, or having security in an emergency. At-will employment can also complicate the process of proving retaliation or discrimination as the reason for a layoff. “Having the at-will rule also makes it really difficult to enforce other work-related laws, like anti-discrimination law,” says Racabi. “If an employer can simply terminate someone without notice, reason, or hearing, it makes proving discriminatory intent extremely hard.” The employer doesn’t have to prove any other justification for the firing. In a 2022 survey from the National Employment Law Project, 69% of U.S. workers who had experienced a layoff or firing reported that they were either given no or an unfair reason. On top of that, 72% of these participants reported being terminated without a chance to improve or any warning. Overall, 66% of workers surveyed stated they support the enactment of just-cause policies. Of course, not everyone thinks at-will employment should be thrown out. Carson Young, an associate professor at West Virginia University’s John Chambers College of Business and Economics, argues that at-will employment is “complicated.” It can allow workers to earn higher salaries and have more flexibility than with a just cause system, since the setup potentially lowers employer costs around hiring extra people, with less incentive to keep anyone onboard. Young also believes that at-will employment grants workers more freedom to leave a job as they please. He also argues that it could also make employers more likely to hire new employees, as they don’t have to make as big of a commitment to the employee if it ends up not being a good fit, a project ends, or the thing they were hired for doesn’t work out. “Employers in [countries] with more job protections are thus more reluctant to hire, because they face greater costs if the hire doesn’t work out,” Young says. How the U.S. compares to other countries The U.S. is fairly unique in having at-will employment, with many other developed countries requiring just cause and notice to terminate an employee. In turn, the individual is often also required to provide notice when leaving a position. “U.S. courts tend to favor freedom of contract and employer-employee flexibility over job security,” says Young. But “employment law in most other countries places a greater emphasis on job security over freedom of contract and flexibility.” In the U.K., arguably the country most directly compared to the U.S., an employer can only let you go for “a valid reason that they can justify” and if they’ve “acted reasonably in the circumstance.” An employer will also typically have to give notice of a layoff between one to 12 weeks prior to termination, depending on the length of employment. An employee must give at least a week’s notice, but it can be longer depending on their contract. Yet, the U.K. also has zero-hour contracts—which mean an employer doesn’t have to guarantee any work and the individual, in turn, doesn’t have to accept any. These casual contracts are common in positions such as retail or hospitality. Critics of the U.K.’s zero-hour contracts point to issues similar to that of at-will employment: Workers on zero-hour contracts “will find it difficult to strategy their ordinary lives and pay their bills because they are guaranteed no shifts and will find they have no regular or fixed income stream,” says David Cabrelli, a professor of labor law at the University of Edinburgh’s Law School. “Seen from the perspective of job and earnings security, both employment-at-will and zero-hours contracts put workers in a very vulnerable and precarious position.” Could the U.S. get rid of at-will employment? The U.K.’s Employment Rights Act 2025 has set new regulations for zero-hour contracts, including a right to guaranteed hours and pay for last-minute shift cancellations. The changes have not yet rolled out, with some employers and unions criticizing the new measures, the Guardian reports. Generally, the U.S. is not typically seen as a country that strongly values workers’ rights, instead valuing the good of the employer or business. But could the U.S. also pursue changes? Some caveats already exist in circumstances such as whistle-blowing or alleging sexual harassment. “However, these exceptions are issue-specific and the legal position could be improved for workers by the introduction of a just cause dismissal regime,” says Cabrelli. So, then, could just cause ever become the law of the land in the U.S.—a place where workers’ rights are rarely prioritized? “At-will is law, and we can change laws,” says Racabi. “We can enact statutory just-cause or procedural mandate laws at the federal, state, and local levels. We can do those without significant legal pushback. Racabi continues: “We can also support unionization; that one of its byproducts is increased workers’ protection via collective bargaining agreements.”  At-will employment might be the norm in the U.S., but that doesn’t mean it’s the best option. Or that it has to be around forever.

We’ve all seen the scene play out in media: A character stands up at work, dramatically declares they quit, and walks out of the office for the last time. While many people will surely empathize with that desire, the reason why a sudden resignation is possible in the U.S. isn’t as great as such a display makes it out to be.

Mostly because it goes both ways: an employer can axe you at the drop of a hat, in theory—even without a warning, PIP, or other chance to improve.

The U.S. has something called at-will employment, which means that you can leave—or lose—your job without giving any notice.

A job that’s at-will “can end at any moment, for good reason, bad reason, or no reason at all, and with no procedural mandates,” claims Gali Racabi, an assistant professor at Cornell’s School of Industrial and Labor Relations and an associated faculty member of Cornell Law School.

At the moment, at-will employment is the law of the land in Washington, D.C., and every U.S. state except Montana.

Despite being the default in America—a country whose culture is associated with entrepreneurialism, independence and one that favors employers without much safety-net protection for workers—at-will employment causes a number of concerns.

That’s a more extreme example. But even losing health insurance without a big medical matter coming up, and no time to find an alternative, can have devastating repercussions around the cost of medicine, seeing a doctor, or having security in an emergency.

At-will employment can also complicate the process of proving retaliation or discrimination as the reason for a layoff.

“Having the at-will rule also makes it really difficult to enforce other work-related laws, like anti-discrimination law,” says Racabi. “If an employer can simply terminate someone without notice, reason, or hearing, it makes proving discriminatory intent extremely hard.” The employer doesn’t have to prove any other justification for the firing.

Recent findings suggest that in a 2022 survey from the National Employment Law Project, 69% of U.S. workers who had experienced a layoff or firing reported that they were either given no or an unfair reason. On top of that, 72% of these participants reported being terminated without a chance to improve or any warning. Overall, 66% of workers surveyed remarked they support the enactment of just-cause policies.

Recent findings suggest that of course, not everyone thinks at-will employment should be thrown out. Carson Young, an associate professor at West Virginia University’s John Chambers College of Business and Economics, argues that at-will employment is “complicated.” It can allow workers to earn higher salaries and have more flexibility than with a just cause system, since the setup potentially lowers employer costs around hiring extra people, with less incentive to keep anyone onboard.

Young also believes that at-will employment grants workers more freedom to leave a job as they please. He also argues that it could also make employers more likely to hire newly introduced employees, as they don’t have to make as big of a commitment to the employee if it ends up not being a good fit, a project ends, or the thing they were hired for doesn’t work out.

“Employers in [countries] with more job protections are thus more reluctant to hire, because they face greater costs if the hire doesn’t work out,” Young says.

The U.S. is fairly unique in having at-will employment, with many other developed countries requiring just cause and notice to terminate an employee. In turn, the individual is often also required to provide notice when leaving a position.

“U.S. courts tend to favor freedom of contract and employer-employee flexibility over job security,” says Young. But “employment law in most other countries places a greater emphasis on job security over freedom of contract and flexibility.”.

In a recent development, in the U.K., arguably the country most directly compared to the U.S., an employer can only let you go for “a valid reason that they can justify” and if they’ve “acted reasonably in the circumstance.” An employer will also typically have to give notice of a layoff between one to 12 weeks prior to termination, depending on the length of employment. An employee must give at least a week’s notice, but it can be longer depending on their contract.

Industry observers note that yet, the U.K. also has zero-hour contracts—which mean an employer doesn’t have to guarantee any work and the individual, in turn, doesn’t have to accept any. These casual contracts are common in positions such as retail or hospitality.

Critics of the U.K.’s zero-hour contracts point to issues similar to that of at-will employment: Workers on zero-hour contracts “will find it difficult to initiative their ordinary lives and pay their bills because they are guaranteed no shifts and will find they have no regular or fixed income stream,” notes David Cabrelli, a professor of labor law at the University of Edinburgh’s Law School.

“Seen from the perspective of job and earnings security, both employment-at-will and zero-hours contracts put workers in a very vulnerable and precarious position.”.

In a recent development, the U.K.’s Employment Rights Act 2025 has set newly introduced regulations for zero-hour contracts, including a right to guaranteed hours and pay for last-minute shift cancellations. The changes have not yet rolled out, with some employers and unions criticizing the new measures, the Guardian reports.

In a recent development, generally, the U.S. is not typically seen as a country that strongly values workers’ rights, instead valuing the good of the employer or business. But could the U.S. also pursue changes?

Some caveats already exist in circumstances such as whistle-blowing or alleging sexual harassment. “However, these exceptions are matter-specific and the legal position could be improved for workers by the introduction of a just cause dismissal regime,” says Cabrelli.

So, then, could just cause ever become the law of the land in the U.S.—a place where workers’ rights are rarely prioritized?

Sources indicate that “At-will is law, and we can change laws,” says Racabi. “We can enact statutory just-cause or procedural mandate laws at the federal, state, and local levels. We can do those without significant legal pushback.

Racabi continues: “We can also support unionization; that one of its byproducts is increased workers’ protection via collective bargaining agreements.”.

At-will employment might be the norm in the U.S., but that doesn’t mean it’s the best option. Or that it has to be around forever.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Utah asked a court to dismiss the criminal charges it filed last month against prediction market operator Kalshi and two of its executives, citing Kalshi’s decision to halt trading in the state that had accused it of running an illegal gambling enterprise.
  • Utah asked a court to dismiss the criminal charges it filed last month against prediction market operator Kalshi and two of its executives, citing Kalshi’s decision to halt trading in the state that had accused it of running an illegal gambling enterprise.
  • The one-sentence motion filed Tuesday in a Salt Lake City-based court by state Attorney General Derek Brown referenced a “change in circumstance.” Brown’s office noted that it could refile the case if Kalshi resumes offering trades on its platform there.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Utah asked a court to dismiss the criminal charges it filed last month against prediction market operator Kalshi and two of its executives, citing Kalshi’s decision to halt trading in the state that had accused it of running an illegal gambling enterprise. The one-sentence motion filed Tuesday in a Salt Lake City-based court by state Attorney General Derek Brown referenced a “change in circumstance.” Brown’s office noted that it could refile the case if Kalshi resumes offering trades on its platform there. “Kalshi has pulled out of Utah, and if it returns, so will the charges,” Brown said in a statement. Utah has been on the front lines of a battle between states and the federal government over who regulates the markets. Litigation has spread across more than 20 states, creating a fragmented legal landscape that analysts say will likely be settled by the U.S. Supreme Court. The felony charges filed by Utah include 13 counts of violating the state’s prohibition on gambling and another charge involving profiting off illegal activity. The state’s charging documents name Kalshi and its cofounders, chief executive officer Tarek Mansour and chief operating officer Luana Lopes Lara. They are due in court in Salt Lake City on December 4, unless a judge agrees to dismiss the case. Utah law prohibits gambling, and Utah considers prediction markets gambling, Brown’s office said. Many other states contend that the platforms’ sports trading activities are flouting their laws that regulate sports betting and casino gambling. Utah’s felony charges represented a latest tactic in how states are trying to assert regulatory authority over the fast-expanding activity. Brown’s office also has asked a court to make Kalshi give up the profits it made in Utah. Kalshi, the nation’s largest prediction market operator, said Monday it had halted trading in Utah after it became clear that a federal judge hearing a case brought by the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) wouldn’t immediately stop Utah’s attempts to shut it down there. A Kalshi spokeswoman called it an “unfortunate outcome for the more than 177,000 Utahns who use Kalshi” but said the company will continue to fight in court for the right to operate in Utah. Kalshi, like the CFTC, argues that prediction markets offer “event contracts” that should be considered swaps under a federal law that grants exclusive regulation to the federal agency. Utah and at least 44 other states have opposed that view. Kalshi sued Utah in February, asking a federal judge to prevent the state from enforcing its gambling restrictions on the platform. A federal judge rejected the request, and an appeal is pending. Trading activity on Kalshi is halted in Nevada and partially in Michigan and Washington, according to Kalshi. —By Marc Levy, Associated Press.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, elon Musk has a new promise: Version 15 of Full Self-Driving drives better than a real driver. “Completely new architecture that deserves being called ‘super’ intelligence, as it drives better than human intelligence,” he wrote on X after Tesla started sending the update to a first batch of owners. That’s great news. It was great news back in November 2023, too, when he wrote: “Over time, Version 12 (end-to-end neural nets) will far exceed human safety even when unsupervised.” Also in August 2025, when he said: “v14 will be better than human for sure, but I don’t know if it will be 10X. Maybe 2X to 3X. v15 has a shot at 10X.” Back then, he offered no data, and no third-party study to support his claim. It’s the same thing now. Tesla states that the new FSD v15—which Musk expects to roll out widely in December—upgrades the neural network that processes the camera sensors into information for the car to drive. It has also swapped the old lo-fi grayscale schematic 3D view for an AI-generated live street scene that looks GTA VI-ish. The latter is the only thing that we know is real—and I have to admit it looks pretty neat—but nobody knows if the new driving engine works as well as Musk claims. [Image: Tesla] Same song, new version number It may not matter too much. The new v15 is still Level 2 autonomous driving, which means drivers will need to watch the road at all times. While Musk says it drives better than a human, it must be a very dumb human because Tesla’s own support page says the software “does not make the vehicle autonomous” and is meant for use “only with a fully attentive driver.” That matters because when a person has to be ready to take over the wheel at any second, every avoided crash is just as much a win for the human as for the machine. FSD v15 now starting to roll out – upgrading every part of the end-to-end driving network Safety25x better handling of safety critical casesTesla Reality View Adds a live visualization of the drive that lets you see & control what FSD is planning to doNavigation for start… pic.twitter.com/Sfjk4wZecW— Tesla (@Tesla) November 21, 2026 Tesla claims that the new FSD offers “25x better handling of safety critical cases.” Better than what? Phil Duan, who leads self-driving at Tesla, said on X that “v15 is 25x safer than v14 across the fleet.” Musk answered an X user, too: “Some people thought we meant 25% improvement; no we mean 25 times!” But we don’t really know about how much “safer” v14 was either. As electric mobility site Electrek points out, without real published figures or a peer-reviewed study—like this one on Waymo reducing its crashes with injured people by 85%—that “25x” claim is hard to substantiate. In a post, the company explains that its new vision encoder—the part of the network that interprets the information from the car’s video cameras—is the reason for that “25x better handling.” Now shared by FSD, Robotaxis, and Optimus humanoids, the engineering team says the new software improves “the critical intervention rate by 25x.” Tesla says the new encoder was trained on “millions of internet videos.” According to Tesla, v15 adjusts its speed better in bad weather and school zones, steers clear of deep standing water, and is quicker to spot signs, potholes, small animals, chains, and junk on the road. It doesn’t say anything about fake Looney Tunes-painted tunnels. It can ease off for speed cameras, too. And it learns from you, so if you cancel the slowdown at the same speed camera twice, by accelerating, it will stop braking at that point of the road. The company also claims that the car’s interior camera—which checks if you are paying attention to the road or not—now works more often when you wear hats and sunglasses. Neat! As part of the update, Tesla Reality View has changed. It now looks very similar to the live situational awareness screens you get in some Chinese cars: a hyperrealistic view of the road and your car as seen from behind at a 45-degree angle. You can see vehicles and people in 3D hyperrealistic renderings. Even the buildings are textured and lit like the real thing. It feels like a high-end car racing game. Musk claims “it’s like GTA.” It looks neat, but it doesn’t seem to convey information better than the older user interface (UI), which showed a much clearer representation of reality. Seen from a high angle, it was a simplified, very stylized version of the road populated with semitransparent versions of vehicles and nearby people. In the old version, despite its perception problems, it was easy to get instant situational awareness. In the new v15, the realism obscures the information with too much darkness and glitz. The interface also features a blue ribbon that traces the route FSD intends to drive, so you can correct it. Chevron arrows float overhead before every turn. And the map now shows several parking spots at your destination. Some Chinese car manufacturers are already displaying this information directly on the windshield, projecting computer-generated wide-screen augmented-reality (AR) graphics over the real world. Fortunately, you can switch to a split view or just pick the GPS map view. Musk claims “you can tap any point on the reality revisualizer to make your car go there.”  Musk says that the new UI uses the same visual features the FSD v15 driving model uses: It’s all AI-generated. The AI model renders short bursts of eight frames at 36 frames per second, using just half of one of the accelerators in the car’s AI4 computer. Still, the video may lag behind reality because the AI is not fast enough. Musk admits the lag is “a bit high due to compute constraints.” He claims Tesla has a way to trim it by about 35%. More promises. If December’s wide release arrives on time (which may or may not happen), it will put the new FSD in a lot more hands. In 2027 we will be able to test the real value of Musk’s promises once again. Let’s stay positive. Maybe this will be it. You know what they say: 15th time’s the charm.

According to recent reports, clips from different generations rarely share resolution, frame rate, or codec settings. Normalise them before joining.

Captions are cheapest when generated from the script and measured clip durations, not transcribed afterwards.

Industry observers note that current video models generate short clips, commonly a handful of seconds each. A longer video is therefore many clips, and every clip is an independent generation. The model has no memory of what the character wore in the previous one.

It has been revealed that that produces three kinds of failure. The character drifts, so hair, clothing, or proportions change between scenes. The style drifts, so lighting and colour grade shift from cut to cut. And the technical specs drift, so one clip is 24 frames per second at one resolution and the next is something else. Each of these is fixable, but only if the project is organised so the fixes can be applied consistently.

Industry observers note that start with a structured storyboard instead of a document full of prompts. One file holds the style, a "character bible", and an ordered list of scenes.

"project": "rainy-day-lantern",.

"setting": "under a bakery awning",.

"action": "finds the lantern glowing on a wooden crate and kneels beside it",.

"camera": "static medium close up",.

"narration": "Then she noticed something glowing under the awning.".

Recent findings suggest that because it is data, a script can check it before you spend any generation credits. Two checks pay for themselves quickly: every character named in a scene must exist in the bible, and no scene may be longer than the clip limit of the model you use.

Never write the per-scene prompt by hand. Generate it, so the style line and the character descriptions are identical every time.

The character description appears word for word in every scene that includes that character. This is the single most effective consistency tactic that needs no special tooling. Changing a detail, say the colour of the boots, becomes one edit in the bible instead of a search through twenty prompts, and the diff reveals exactly what changed between versions.

Put the style line first and keep it identical across all scenes.

It has been revealed that describe one action per clip. Two sequential actions in one prompt often produce a blend of both.

Sources indicate that keep camera directions simple. A single move per clip is more reliable than a combination.

Avoid naming real people, brands, or existing characters in prompts. Beyond the rights issue, it makes results harder to reproduce.

Recent findings suggest that clips from separate generations often disagree on resolution, frame rate, pixel format, or codec parameters. Joining them directly can produce stutters, green frames, or an outright error. Convert every clip to one agreed format first.

-vf "scale=1280:720:force_original_aspect_ratio=decrease,pad=1280:720:(ow-iw)/2:(oh-ih)/2,fps=24,format=yuv420p" \.

-an -c:v libx264 -crf 18 "norm/$(basename "$f")".

In a recent development, the filter scales each clip to fit a 1280 by 720 frame, adds padding if the aspect ratio differs, sets 24 frames per second, and forces a widely compatible pixel format. The -an flag drops any audio the model generated, since narration will be added as one track later. Name clips with zero padded numbers such as s01.mp4 and s02.mp4, so a shell glob sorts them in story order.

Once every file shares the same parameters, the concat demuxer can join them without re-encoding:.

for f in norm/*.mp4; do echo "file '$PWD/$f'"; done > list.txt.

ffmpeg -y -f concat -safe 0 -i list.txt -c copy stitched.mp4.

Sources indicate that hard cuts are the safe default. Crossfades are possible with ffmpeg's xfade filter, but they require careful offset arithmetic and a re-encode, so add them only when a cut genuinely looks wrong.

It has been revealed that captions are easiest when they come from the script, not from a speech recognition pass over the finished video. The storyboard already holds the narration text and each scene's length, so an SRT file is a few lines of code. Use measured durations rather than planned ones, because a generated clip is often a little shorter or longer than requested.

According to recent reports, everything above is a good fit when you need repeatability: many videos from templates, versioned storyboards, automated publishing, or tight control over the model. The price is that you own the glue code, the ffmpeg settings, and the failures.

According to recent reports, for one off projects, or when the people making the video are not developers, a managed platform is often the more sensible choice. Tools such as magiclight.ai bundle story to video generation, character handling, voice, and an editor in one interface, and advertise videos of up to 50 minutes. Check the specifics yourself, because claims like that are marketing, and results depend on your content. One point matters for developers in particular: if you need to automate generation from your own code, confirm that the platform you pick offers an API or export route before you build a workflow around it. A tool with a good editor and no programmatic access suits a different job than the pipeline in this article.

A short manual pass catches what automation does not. Watch the whole video once at normal speed, looking only at continuity. Read the captions against the audio. Check that no real person's likeness, brand mark, or protected character slipped into the footage. Finally, check the disclosure rules of the platform you publish on, since many now ask creators to label realistic synthetic media, and the rules change.

Industry observers note that the model is only one component of a long-form AI video. The reliability comes from the structure around it: a validated storyboard, prompts generated from it, clips forced into one format, and captions derived from measured data. Each of those is ordinary software engineering, and none of it depends on which generation model you choose, so the pipeline survives when the model changes.

Start with a two minute video and four or five scenes. Fix the seams there before scaling up, because every continuity problem you find at that size is one you will not have to hunt for in a ten minute project.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The public reaction to Jensen Huang’s return has been mixed at best, raising the hackles of lawmakers and corporate governance experts.
  • The public reaction to Jensen Huang’s return has been mixed at best, raising the hackles of lawmakers and corporate governance experts.
  • Sources indicate that in videos circulating across social media, Huang received a hero’s welcome at Nvidia headquarters, where his employees lined the walls and staircases as they cheered for him.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The public reaction to Jensen Huang’s return has been mixed at best, raising the hackles of lawmakers and corporate governance experts. Even the stock price took a bit of a dip after surging by over 30% on Monday. Within the company, however, the mood appears to be considerably lighter. In videos circulating across social media, Huang received a hero’s welcome at Nvidia headquarters, where his employees lined the walls and staircases as they cheered for him. Between chants of “Jensen! Jensen!” and “We love you Jensen,” he addressed his staff in a display of contrition. “I’m terribly sorry for putting all of you through all of this,” he stated. “I’ve made some very terrible mistakes, and I’m going to work on coming back.” After an employee threw her arms around Huang in a tight hug—lasting over 10 seconds—he continued: “Thank you all for the second chance. I’m going to be a better CEO the second time around.” Many Nvidia employees have taken to LinkedIn to express their relief over Huang’s return, seemingly overlooking the indiscretions that led to his ousting. They heaped praise on their newly reinstated CEO, describing him as the “heartbeat of Nvidia” and “one of a kind.”  One employee even invoked Charles Dickens, paraphrasing the opening of A Tale of Two Cities: “It was the worst of times, it is the best of times. It was the season of Darkness, it is the season of Light. It was the winter of despair, it is the spring of hope. We had nothing before us, we have everything before us.” Another employee claimed he always knew Huang would return to Nvidia: “When Jensen stepped down, many said their goodbyes and thanked him for his legacy. I stayed quiet—not out of indifference, but because deep down I knew there is only one boss, and he would be back.” A former robotics engineer at Nvidia who quit rather publicly after Huang’s resignation congratulated him and admitted he made a hasty decision. “Looking back, I may have moved too promptly, and I don’t want to rush into another major decision. For now, I’d like to take some time to rest, reflect, and think carefully about my future. As part of that, I’m open to exploring the possibility of returning.” These reactions line up with previous reports about employee sentiment after Huang stepped down: According to Wired, many employees showed immediate support for him internally, asking the board to reverse the decision. More than 10,000 current Nvidia employees, or about a quarter of its workforce, signed a petition to reinstate Huang as CEO. Still, there are some employees who seem to feel differently—perhaps those who have been the target of Huang’s outbursts and creative insults, as reported by the Newly introduced York Times recently. In a Wired report this week, several current and former employees expressed frustration over the turn of events, in part because they had hoped Huang’s exit would usher in some long overdue changes. A number of employees were disturbed by Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy and at least one inappropriate relationship with an employee. Beyond that, however, they also felt that Nvidia condoned abusive behavior and echoed previous claims that Huang belittled employees at times. (In an internal post, one employee asserted: “If Jensen comes back, I’m not doing any HR trainings ever again.”) Workers also told Wired that the focus on unity and the “one team” ethos discouraged employees from challenging leadership. Even employees who have few misgivings about the culture may now find themselves questioning Huang’s leadership. One engineering leader openly grappled with his feelings about Huang in a LinkedIn post, before he was reinstated. “Some believe his contributions to NVIDIA and the industry are so extraordinary that he deserves another chance,” he wrote. “Others argue that making exceptions for powerful leaders sets a dangerous precedent. I’ve wrestled with this question all week. My opinion has probably changed every single day. And I’ve realized something. I don’t have a clear answer.” As evidenced by the reception to Huang yesterday, this may not be the prevailing view among employees. But whether or not other employees have lost faith in Huang, there are now open questions about how—if at all—the company prepares to address the myriad complications that have been exposed by the events of the last few weeks.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Business culture has long lionized bold, disruptive leaders. But these days, at least, Americans are yearning for some stability. In a survey conducted shortly after the midterm elections, 82% of Americans stated they prefer leaders who “get things back to normal rather than shake things up” and 82% also said they prefer a “stable and predictable” life. The global public relations firm Burson interviewed about 1,600 Americans across party lines. The poll was published November 14. Ninety percent of respondents also said they want honest, calm, consistent leadership (90%), and 75% said they lose respect for CEOs who change positions under pressure. It is easy to interpret these findings as a reflection of current public opinion about President Donald Trump. Trump’s penchant for disruption and brash businessman image helped him win the White House twice, but the outcome of the midterms—and the results of the Burson survey—indicate that the public has grown tired of the chaos. A survey of roughly 100,000 midterm voters found that about two-thirds thought Trump had the wrong priorities, while seven in 10 said Congress hasn’t been doing enough to check the president’s power. As Fast Firm reported earlier this month, the midterm results also illustrate the risks organizations run when they become overly dependent on a charismatic leader. A leader’s success can make subordinates increasingly reluctant to question their judgment, even when circumstances change. “At some point, you have to ask whether people are following your vision, or simply afraid to challenge it,” leadership expert Adam Mendler said.

Streaming in 1080p will be the default in Google Meet, regardless of whether you pay for Google Workspace. That includes personal Google Accounts.

Sources indicate that google states people will default to sending and receiving 1080p video, at the minimum. Previously, Google Meet made 720p the standard for streaming, and a higher resolution had historically been locked behind the Google One 2TB plan. That’s been true since 1080p streaming was rolled out in 2023.

The upgrade will roll out to everyone, including those with Google Workspace accounts and personal Google Accounts. The only requirement to stream your own 1080p video in Google Meet for web will be hardware-based. Google’s press release states that devices with cameras capable of streaming in high definition will do so, and the feature will be turned on automatically.

Sources indicate that it can be disabled, though. People can head to Settings > Video in Google Meet for web. Video will also appear in a lower resolution if the user’s video tile is shrunk down on-screen.

In a recent development, the upgrade appears to be centered on web-only instances of Google Meet, and might not include the app on Android or iOS. For the time being, those versions may still be limited to streaming in 720p for those who don’t have an active Google One subscription.

Google Meet started its extended rollout of 1080p streaming to everyone earlier this month, so it shouldn’t be much longer until the change has taken place completely.

💡 Key Takeaways
